settings.heading: The water comes off the road, not the sky.
settings.lede: Overshoes seal everywhere except the one place the water actually arrives, and there is nowhere at the office to dry a cycling shoe before the ride home.
settings.image_alt: Cycling & Commuting in HydroSox waterproof socks

settings.heading: Two rides, one pair of shoes.
settings.lede: A wet commute is not one event. It is a wet ride in, eight hours of a shoe not drying under a desk, and a wet ride home in the same kit.

settings.title: Spray travels upward
settings.body: Most of what soaks a rider comes off the front wheel and the road surface, aimed straight at the ankle and the shoe opening.

settings.title: Overshoes leak where they close
settings.body: They are cut to go over a shoe, which means an opening at the ankle — which is exactly where the spray is going.

settings.title: Nothing dries at the office
settings.body: A cycling shoe under a desk for eight hours is a cycling shoe that is still wet at half past five.

settings.heading: Waterproofing that stays on the foot.
settings.head_note: Sealing a shoe from the outside is a losing geometry. This seals the foot instead, and the foot is inside all of it.

settings.title: The barrier is inside the shoe
settings.body: Spray that gets through the shoe or past an overshoe stops at the sock. What the shoe does or does not do stops being the deciding factor.

settings.title: It works with the shoes you ride in
settings.body: No cleat compatibility to check and nothing to stretch over a sole. It goes under whatever you already clip or lace into.

settings.title: It comes inside with you
settings.body: You are not carrying a wet overshoe around the building. The sock comes off with the rest of your kit.

settings.heading: The same pair, in the conditions this page is about.
settings.head_note: Product imagery rather than a documentary shoot, so read it for what the sock is and where it goes — not as evidence. The checkable claim is the membrane.

settings.caption: Stopped at the café, still in the kit
settings.image_alt: Stopped at the café, still in the kit

settings.title: Crew height clears a shoe collar
settings.body: The cuff sits above the top of most cycling and commuting shoes, so the sock's opening is not level with the shoe's.

settings.title: A spare pair in the bag is the whole plan
settings.body: Change at the far end and the ride home starts dry. That is lighter and cheaper than a second pair of shoes.

settings.title: Cool wash, air dry
settings.body: They are back in the rotation the next morning without needing a dryer.

settings.heading: Where the geometry still wins.
settings.body: Water above the cuff gets in, and once it is in, the sock holds it about as well as it kept it out. On a commute that means kerbside puddles rather than a flooded lane.
